source_document.body:
Severe weather conditions have become constant. Cyclones, storms, heatwaves, floods, and droughts continue to put critical infrastructure, homes, livelihoods, and lives at risk in the U.S. and around the world.
Heat waves and droughts are the second-deadliest weather category, causing critical infrastructure instability, power line inefficiency, thermal sagging, and overloaded transformers that can lead to load shedding or automatically shut down critical systems. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency ( CISA ) recorded 2023 as “the fifth-warmest year in the 129-year record for the country as a whole.”
COMMENTARY
Nationwide, heat waves turning into heat domes are becoming annual occurrences as the frequency of high-temperature days and peak heat conditions rise year over year.
Monitoring Solutions for Critical Infrastructure Operations
According to the N1Critical stats , interrupted operations at healthcare facilities cost more than “$600,000 per hour ($7,500/minute) with delayed care, emergency diversions ($8,000–$13,000/hour), and lost surgical volume.” Interruptions in manufacturing facilities can cost an average of about $260,000 per hour with “halting production lines and idle labor.” In data centers, downtime costs range between “ $300,000 to $540,000 per hour ($9,000/minute), driven by customer churn, data recovery, and SLA penalties.”
To maintain uninterrupted operations, critical infrastructure organizations need solutions that can provide proactive monitoring and alerting of all key components in mechanical and electrical systems. Continuous monitoring provides engineers and operators with real-time views of equipment and systems and ensures optimal operations regardless of outdoor conditions.
IIoT and SCADA platforms enable teams to monitor and analyze data from different sources over time with real-time alerts and actionable insights that expedite tactical equipment repairs without on-site manual equipment and systems inspection. Live data reports also help detect and address deviations from standard conditions before equipment failures. This allows engineers and operators to proactively deploy resources as needed to prevent downtime.
Extreme Heat Jeopardizes Grid Stability
Extreme heat not only drives electricity demand to record highs; it also dramatically strains all aspects of the grid. Surging temperatures affect the entire infrastructure ecosystem, starting from power generation plants and extending to local distribution lines.
When grids are strained, demands increase, and systems’ efficiencies drop as grid operators face near-record loads. With air conditioners, electric vehicles (EVs), and other energy-intensive systems operating continuously in both residential and commercial settings, electricity consumption surges, increasing demands on the power grid. Extended high temperatures also decrease the efficiency of transmission lines, transformers, and substations, which need higher energy levels to power in-house temperature-sensitive industrial cooling systems.
This past July, an hourly peak load in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), the regional transmission organization serving most of Texas, broke a record of 91.1 gigawatts (GW), according to data reported by Hourly Electric Grid Monitor . The PJM Interconnection, the grid serving 67 million customers in 13 mid-Atlantic states, reported that power demand hit 162 GW around 6 p.m. on July 2 — the second-highest level ever recorded by PJM.
To avoid blackouts , local utilities and cooperatives nationwide issue public alerts requesting their utility customers to stop using major appliances and conserve electricity during peak afternoon and evening hours. Commercial consumers are requested and, in some cases, mandated to shed load during peak periods. The U.S. Department of Energy has authorized emergency orders that allow grid operators to direct large energy users like data centers to switch to backup generation supplies before declaring severe emergency alerts.
Preemptive Safeguards of Critical Infrastructure
With frequent, longer-lasting heat waves, organizations must consider comprehensive monitoring systems that can integrate seamlessly across portfolio sites, existing systems, and devices. To avoid costly consequences, operators can be preemptive with preventive maintenance of legacy and new equipment, systems, and devices to eliminate major failures and costly shutdowns.
A failure in the cooling system can cause equipment to overheat, resulting in a controlled shutdown to prevent complete equipment failure. When equipment goes down, services to end-users at data centers, telecom towers, utility distribution centers, and other locations will lag, interrupting or delaying automated and digitized services like banking, fueling your vehicle, internet searches, or using electrical appliances.
Ongoing heat waves also cause load increases in operational systems. Without constant monitoring of operating parameters and fault indicators, operators risk more frequent maintenance and higher costs. Operating systems at higher loads may seem like a good short-term solution, but it increases energy consumption and, in the long run, causes premature failure of system components, drastically raising operating costs.
Organizations with new mechanical systems should consider a redesign to optimize operational efficiency in higher ambient temperatures. Operators must closely monitor newly installed high-efficiency mechanical systems and existing HVAC and cooling configurations, which can’t handle rising ambient temperatures without a complete redesign.
Rising temperatures decrease the efficiency of air-cooled condensers. And since newer systems operate with tighter tolerances, their performance can drop more rapidly with increasing ambient temperature limits. To prevent thermal overload, modern equipment needs adjusted refrigerant charges and precise airflow. Upgrading fans and ductwork can improve higher air volumes and heat rejection capability.
Engineers designing systems must consider their equipment limitations relative to overall system capabilities. To avoid system failures during extreme weather conditions, engineers should:
Use regionally updated weather data when calculating their cooling loads. Historical weather averages are unreliable as conditions shift drastically.
Choose units with wider coil surface areas for ambient operations to help upsize condenser capacity to meet rising heat waves.
Better ventilation, in mechanical rooms or rooftop airflow, can release trapped heat that accumulates around equipment.
Optimize controls by using smart staging controls to manage compressors with multi-stage or variable speeds.
Drastic weather conditions are becoming common. Protecting critical infrastructure during such periods can be managed with real-time data monitoring solutions that track all connected equipment and systems and allow preemptive measures to ensure uninterrupted operations.
— Dave Schaible is COO of Radix IoT , with three decades of experience in the automation, controls, and monitoring industry, specializing in data centers and mission-critical facility applications.

source_document.body:
As the freight industry heads into its highest-volume stretch of the year, the cargo theft numbers tell a deceptively reassuring story. Reported incidents fell sharply in the second quarter of 2026, down roughly a quarter from the year before. But losses over that same period more than doubled , to $304.6 million, with the average theft now running about $564,000. Industry estimates suggest only about 10% of incidents ever get reported at all.
Those numbers tell a story about the state of the industry. Ahead of his presentations at this year’s F3: Future of Freight Festival , we sat down with Aqil Naeem, co-founder and CEO of E3 Group , to hear his perspective on the situation. “There are fewer thefts, but each one costs a lot more,” Naeem said. The drop, he explained, is due to a shift in tactics as bad actors adjust to the industry’s defenses.
“Fictitious pickups barely moved while overall theft events fell,” Naeem said. “Criminals are stealing less often and choosing their loads more carefully.” The takeaway for brokers and shippers heading into Q4, he said, is that a quieter quarter on paper isn’t a safer quarter.
What’s driving the shift, according to Naeem, is how cheap and accessible the tools of impersonation have become.
“A thief can order fake license plates or carrier decals and have them tomorrow, then stick a magnetic carrier name over the real one on the truck door,” Naeem said. “They can buy a carrier’s email login on the dark web and send pickup instructions from the real inbox. They can generate a photo of a truck or a CDL with AI in seconds.” It’s a pattern E3 Group sees repeating across the industry: phishing campaigns and remote-access malware used to take over business emails and carrier accounts.
The transition from smash-and-grab theft to deception-based fraud is why E3 Group built its platform around verifying the person behind the wheel rather than just the paperwork behind the load. Naeem said the economics of organized freight crime have simply gotten too easy.
“The tools of organized crime have never been easier to get,” Naeem said of the shift toward strategic theft. “A fake CDL with barcodes that actually scan can be ordered online. A carrier’s email password can be bought on the dark web. A convincing photo of a truck or a document takes seconds with AI.” Put together, he said, a fictitious pickup can be run from anywhere with a laptop. “It pays better than breaking into a trailer, and the thief never has to set foot in the yard,” he said.
Naeem described impersonation as having matured into “systematic business,” with criminal groups taking over carrier email and compliance accounts. In some cases, they simply buy real carrier companies outright. “The weak point has moved from the trailer lock to identity,” he said. “Most vetting still checks the carrier on paper and never checks the person who actually shows up for the freight.”
Verifying the driver, not just the paperwork
That gap is exactly what E3 Driver Authentication , the company’s driver verification product, is designed to close. Naeem walked through how the process works in practice: “When a driver is assigned to a load, they get a text with a link. There’s no app to download.” From there, he said, they take a few live photos: their CDL, the side of the truck, the cab card, and a selfie, and the system runs those inputs against more than 50 signals in seconds, returning what Naeem called “a clear go or no-go with the recorded proof behind it.” Through it all, the broker always makes the final call.
[Credit: E3 Group]
Among the fraud patterns the platform has caught, Naeem pointed to magnetic decals stuck over a truck’s real carrier markings, AI-generated or edited CDL and truck images, and driver switch-outs between authentication and arrival. The system also cross-references the barcode on the back of a CDL against the front of the card, controls the phone’s camera so nobody can upload a recycled photo (Naeem said the platform once flagged a CDL that had been photographed off a tablet screen), and checks VINs across the cab card, door-jamb sticker,and the broker’s own records, alongside location data pulled from cell tower, GPS and IP sources.
The timing matters as much as the checks themselves. “It happens hours before pickup, not at the dock,” Naeem said. “If something’s off, the broker or shipper has time to put a different carrier on the load before the truck ever shows up.”
E3’s answer to the newest wave of fraud tactics is a layered approach that can catch out AI voice cloning and spoofed motor carrier numbers. Caleb Sirak, the company’s co-founder and president, said the platform can distinguish human speech from generated audio, but added that the company doesn’t lean on phone verification in the first place.
“A cloned voice can get through a call,” Sirak said. “It can’t produce a live photo of a real CDL whose barcode matches its front, a face that matches that CDL, or a truck whose VINs match across three sources.” The same skepticism applies to carrier credentials. “Owning the MC is only the starting point,” Sirak said. “We don’t take anything at face value.” Even geography gets checked. If a verification link is sent for a Texas pickup and opened in Kentucky, for instance, E3 Group flags it right away.
The most common vetting mistake
Much of what makes fictitious pickups work, Sirak said, comes down to a basic conflation in how carriers get vetted in the first place. Treating a carrier check as a driver check”is the most common mistake he sees. A broker confirms a motor carrier number, operating authority and insurance, and all of it checks out clean, but a thief who has taken over a real carrier’s account passes every one of those checks.
Identity verification, meanwhile, often gets reduced to the weakest link, such as a phone call or a photo texted in.
“A $25 fake CDL with working barcodes will pass a visual check,” Naeem said, adding that asking for ID over the phone or by email creates legal exposure without making anyone safer. The result, as he put it: “You end up with proof of the carrier and no proof of who’s actually behind the wheel.”
Preparing for peak season
Heading into the holiday stretch, Naeem pointed to a combination of pressures.
“Peak season combines high-value freight, heavy volume and thin staffing,” Naeem said, calling November and December the highest-risk months of the year. With teams stretched thin, he said, “no one has time to double check a carrier, so a thief posing as one gets waived through.”
According to Naeem, there are two steps that cost nothing to implement, even without dedicated fraud technology in place. “Don’t release the pickup number until you know who’s coming,” he said, describing the most reliable manual workaround E3 has encountered in the field: “a FaceTime call with the driver, standing at the truck, on every high-value or theft-prone load before the pickup number goes out.”
The second step is sourcing discipline. Pull insurance and authority records directly from issuing bodies rather than trusting uploaded documents, and call back only on numbers already on file, not numbers you just got from an email signature. Formalizing those habits matters just as much as the habits themselves, according to Naeem, who recommended writing identity checks into a standing SOP and naming, in advance, who has authority to approve last-minute changes to pickup or delivery instructions.
E3’s own platform, Naeem said, is designed to take the manual version of that work off a team’s plate. “E3 driver authentication automates the first step on every load,” he said, noting it integrates with existing transportation management systems and can be running in a day.
A widening gap between targeted freight and everyday loads
The numbers show that criminals are increasingly selective about what they target. It changes the math for shippers when it comes to high-value goods like electronics and copper.
“Criminals operate on a tradeoff between the value of the freight compared to the effort of stealing it,” Naeem said, pointing to shippers who have seen their driver rejection rate fall after adopting E3’s verification process. “By elevating the cost of stealing your freight relative to the market, criminals are disincentivized from stealing your cargo,” he said.
Case in point, Naeem told us about a high-value automotive shipper that, before implementing E3 Shield, had lost multiple loads to fraud. After onboarding, the platform caught a cluster of repeated attempts from the same region using doctored CDLs with falsified expiration dates and misrepresented domicile status, including one case where a fraudster submitted a doctored CDL front paired with a real CDL back in an attempt to beat the system.
“After a month of these attempts being thwarted, we stopped seeing them attempt to get our customer’s freight,” Naeem said. Company-wide, he added, “there has not been a single theft on an E3-verified load,” a claim the company backs with a full fee-refund guarantee.
Where fraud prevention goes from here
The fight against freight fraud is shifting from document-based checks toward continuous identity verification across a shipment’s entire life cycle.
“Technology can keep pace, but only if it stops relying on documents and phone calls,” Naeem said. “The industry needs identity checks throughout the life of a shipment, not just at tender .” He outlined three changes he expects to take hold industry-wide: authentication at every handoff rather than just the first one, clear pass/fail decisions instead of ambiguous risk scores, and audit trails detailed enough for legal teams to rely on in place of today’s ad hoc verification calls.
The technology itself improves with scale. “E3 driver authentication gets better the more drivers we see,” Naeem said. “We’ve done more than 700,000 driver authentications, and every one makes the next check sharper.” Given that individual companies can’t stop crime or fraud as a whole, the goal is to make a given shipper’s freight a harder target. “We stop fictitious pickups before the truck reaches the dock,” Naeem said. “Every load gets the same check, every result is logged, and the broker gets proof of who picked up the freight. That makes your freight harder to steal than the next load, so the thieves move on.”

A Massachusetts man who repeatedly failed commercial driving exams now faces federal charges involving a Bluetooth cheating scheme . Investigators accuse Rudy Romero Nolasco, 42, of receiving answers through a concealed earpiece during his commercial learner’s permit examination. Phone records connected his testing activity to Frank Castro, who later received a federal conviction. Prosecutors announced the charges on October 15, 2026, nearly five years after the alleged misconduct.
Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles records show Nolasco failed three sets of commercial driving examinations in January 2016. Those tests covered general knowledge, combination vehicles and air brake requirements. On November 23, 2021, he passed all three subjects. The following month, he returned for additional examinations covering tanker trucks and double or triple trailers.
Undercover investigation uncovers $3,000 cheating arrangement
The investigation began taking shape in October 2021 when Castro contacted an undercover Homeland Security Investigations agent. Castro offered to help the agent obtain a commercial learner’s permit for $3,000. He requested identification documents, partial Social Security information and medical certification records to schedule the examination. Castro also indicated he had previously helped other applicants obtain permits.
On November 23, 2021, Nolasco began his examination at 10:58 a.m. Castro called him one minute later, according to T-Mobile records. The test ended at 11:36 a.m., but their conversation continued until 11:38 a.m. Homeland Security Investigations Special Agent Timothy Taber documented the overlapping times in a 10-page federal affidavit.
On December 10, 2021, Castro explained the cheating method to the undercover investigator. Applicants would conceal Bluetooth earpieces beneath headphones provided at Registry of Motor Vehicles testing centers. Someone outside the testing facility could hear examination questions and provide answers through the hidden equipment. Investigators recorded conversations describing how the arrangement worked.
Nolasco returns for additional endorsement exams
On December 16, 2021, Nolasco returned for additional commercial driving qualifications. He passed the tanker endorsement examination but failed the test covering double and triple trailers. Investigators also identified a $1,800 withdrawal from his account and matching deposit into Castro’s account. Authorities could not determine the exact transfer method.
On December 17, 2021, he passed the double and triple trailer test in nine minutes. The examination began at 9:42 a.m. and ended at 9:51 a.m. Telephone records show Castro called five minutes before testing began. Their conversation ended at the exact time Nolasco completed the examination.
Later that day, Castro directed the undercover agent toward Nolasco for help with the cheating equipment. On December 21, 2021, both men met at a McDonald’s restaurant in Lynn, Massachusetts. Nolasco demonstrated how to conceal the earpiece, communicate with Castro and avoid detection. He supplied the equipment and acknowledged paying for assistance during his own examinations.
On December 22, 2021, the undercover agent deposited $3,000 into Castro’s Eastern Bank account. Investigators then conducted a controlled examination at the Danvers Registry of Motor Vehicles. Castro instructed the agent to sit in the far-right corner, away from the testing center’s camera view. The agent received answers remotely, passed the examination and obtained a commercial learner’s permit.
A technical problem prevented investigators from recording the telephone conversation during the controlled examination. However, authorities had previously recorded discussions explaining the cheating arrangement. Financial records and undercover observations provided additional evidence. Investigators used those findings to support the federal case.
Federal prosecution raises additional questions
A federal grand jury indicted Castro in April 2024 for his role in the scheme. A jury convicted him in January 2026. On May 1, 2026, a federal judge sentenced Castro to time served , approximately 23 months in custody. Federal prosecutors subsequently brought charges against Nolasco.
Nolasco appeared in federal court in Boston on October 13, 2026, and received conditional release. The charge of unlawfully producing an identification document carries up to 15 years in prison. Federal law also permits three years of supervised release and a fine reaching $250,000.
Homeland Security Investigations conducted the investigation with assistance from the U.S. Department of Transportation Office of Inspector General. Assistant U.S. Attorney David Tobin of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case. Investigators have not established how many other applicants participated in Castro’s operation. Available court records also leave unanswered whether Nolasco eventually obtained a full commercial driver’s license. The records do not establish whether other participants drove commercial trucks after obtaining permits through the scheme. Nolasco remains presumed innocent unless proven guilty.
Why It Matters
Commercial driving examinations establish mandatory knowledge requirements before applicants can advance toward operating heavy vehicles. This investigation documents how concealed communications equipment allowed an undercover applicant to bypass that testing process.

retained_collection_events.source_quote: Investigators accuse Rudy Romero Nolasco, 42, of receiving answers through a concealed earpiece during his commercial learner’s permit examination.
Undercover investigation uncovers $3,000 cheating arrangement
The investigation began taking shape in October 2021 when Castro contacted an undercover Homeland Security Investigations agent.
Castro offered to help the agent obtain a commercial learner’s permit for $3,000.
He requested identification documents, partial Social Security information and medical certification records to schedule the examination.
Castro also indicated he had previously helped other applicants obtain permits.
Homeland Security Investigations Special Agent Timothy Taber documented the overlapping times in a 10-page federal affidavit.
On December 10, 2021, Castro explained the cheating method to the undercover investigator.
Investigators recorded conversations describing how the arrangement worked.
Investigators also identified a $1,800 withdrawal from his account and matching deposit into Castro’s account.
Investigators then conducted a controlled examination at the Danvers Registry of Motor Vehicles.
The agent received answers remotely, passed the examination and obtained a commercial learner’s permit.
A technical problem prevented investigators from recording the telephone conversation during the controlled examination.
Investigators used those findings to support the federal case.
Federal law also permits three years of supervised release and a fine reaching $250,000.
Homeland Security Investigations conducted the investigation with assistance from the U.S. Department of Transportation Office of Inspector General.
Investigators have not established how many other applicants participated in Castro’s operation.
The records do not establish whether other participants drove commercial trucks after obtaining permits through the scheme.
This investigation documents how concealed communications equipment allowed an undercover applicant to bypass that testing process.

By Erik Muttersbach, Founder & CEO,Fabian Struck, CCO, Christopher Hoegner, Head of Deployments, Zauber
20 October 2026
Agentic process execution could change the P&L far beyond productivity, and the real gains for forwarders sit in execution quality, margin capture and a new kind of moat.
“Innovation and productivity are at the core of what we do.” That was the slogan by a global TMS provider in 2016. In the rear-view mirror, most of the innovation has barely moved the needle from a top-down perspective. Productivity of 40 to 60 files remains a common market result. Even if there were some gains, they might have been absorbed: more reports to be maintained, more customer-specific processes to be executed.
Ten years on, you will find that claim on every billboard again. However, within the last 24 months, first movers are already realising tangible upside. Large incumbents DSV and K&N do not shy away from concrete, public impact commitments of 3-digit million dollar amounts or individual players pretend to cross the 100 monthly files per person mark.
So it is worth reviewing the substance behind, and, more importantly, what it implies in the wider context of the industry.
Tackling the AI potential
Based on our own experience from building Forto and working with many of the leading global forwarders, we reviewed end-to-end processes of up to 100 steps each: the time each requires, its automation potential, and the time that remains manual: the automation estimates came out up to 82%. We see an evolution of the sources of AI automation over time currently (see graphic).
1. Standard automation through data entry into the system (month 0-12): The obvious one, and where many companies start. Examples: turning a customer’s booking email into a booking, updating events or documents or keying commercial invoice and bill of lading data into the system. It sounds simple, but companies will have to build conviction into AI with this first step in our experience, and can’t skip it.
2. Orchestration across fragmented systems and rules to deliver better customer processes (month 6-18): Here the work is not copying data but combining sources and applying logic. Quotation is the classic case. The agent pulls rates from carrier sheets and contracts, rate management systems, adds surcharges, applies customer-specific margin rules, checks capacity and assembles the quote. Other examples are cross-checking documents against the booking, and matching carrier invoices to accruals, orchestrating communication and documentation.
3. Coordinating activities that carry their own process knowledge and, hence, deliver customer value beyond (month 18 and beyond): These build on the first two, but they also need an understanding of the process itself, plus the judgment to run it. Examples: handling a delayed or rolled shipment end to end by informing the customer, orchestrating POs and SKU visibility, rebooking and adjusting costs, and monitoring demurrage and detention before charges accrue.
AI automation finally correlates with other business outcomes
Different than in the past, productivity and automation now works hand in hand with the other goals in the forwarder’s P&L.
Topline and the ability to compete on prices. Obviously faster and more accurate pricing execution has an impact on win-rates. That is not new. However, in the past, productivity gains have rarely translated into pricing leeway. With material AI cost gains, the automation lever has the potential to change the industry. In a tender where $10 on a submitted rate card decides on the actual nomination, a cost advantage of $50, $70 or $100 per file changes the ability to price
competitively.
Profitability . Typical gross profit margins range between 15-25%. That makes the gap between two kinds of forwarders decisive: those who extract the last dollar out of every file, and those who can’t afford to. A larger part of a file’s profit sits in execution, not in the quote or the final invoice. It comes from picking the right partner, watching demurrage and detention closely and keeping accruals actively managed, billing every surcharge. Today that is partly leakage. A well-instructed agent applies the same discipline to every file, it reads the full context from emails, TMS and then follows exactly your process every time, also in peak times or when human operators are flooded with additional work during transport disruptions.
Customer experience. The trade-off was customization versus automation. Agents execute what they are instructed to no matter how standardized the instructions are, so capturing a customer’s context now becomes a one-off task. It enables consistent execution on an individual level. We found in a recent analysis that up to 30% of relevant customer information comes from the customer’s context, such as SOPs, the actual eMail or documents. Building on this context allows forwarders to serve shippers whose requirements used to be too complex to serve profitably, or to replicate their best service levels across regions, segments and products. Even further, capabilities like SOP monitoring in combination with AI exception handling will enable forwarders to get a closer grip on their process and data quality itself.
Fast forward: Potential implications
Together these effects can potentially double the operating result and, therefore, change the economics of the business model, especially for those at the frontier who are implementing. Looking at a typical forwarder P&L, one can hypothesise that about 60% of the impact traces back to productivity itself. The other 40% sits on the top line and gross profit line, through better execution and less leakage.
1. A material EBIT upside that changes how forwarders are valued. The upside is large enough to change the logic by which companies are valued and evaluated, and the gap between frontier players and the rest will show up in the numbers. Should the productivity gain lead to pricing effects, there is no optionality for the broader market to optimize its operational cost base accordingly with AI automation.
2. The automation gains compound end-to-end. There is good reason to believe that productivity gains in this space will perpetuate themselves. Every automated process produces more context, cleaner data and sharper instructions, which makes the next process easier to automate. It also amplifies the risk profile of early choices: point solutions and the lack of an end-to-end view can become a liability, and what gets built in the early stage can turn into legacy surprisingly fast.
3. Standard process execution is not a differentiator. When players can execute reliably, excellent individual execution is no longer a craft that sets anyone apart. It also exposes niche customization: if you have been winning on a high-customization niche, expect competition from players who can deliver the same customization at lower cost.
4. The operator’s role will change. The focus moves from execution to judgment and expertise work. People spend their time on exceptions, as they do today. Many say freight forwarding is a “people business”, and this will continue. But the capability organisations need to build changes. The ability to abstract and conceptualise a process, which is what now goes into the prompts and instructions of the AI alongside them, becomes crucial for successful, widespread adoption.
5. The moat shifts to orchestration and context. From a technology perspective, the moat used to be data availability and a high-quality system of record. Now it is orchestrating fragmented data sources and abstracting process understanding and excellence to a level an agentic co-worker can execute. At the same time, customization becomes an imperative, and companies will invest in and extend its contextual layer. Much of what drives operations today is hidden in unstructured data: notes fields, long documents, tribal knowledge. It will become explicit.
Productivity has been the promise for ten years. What is new is that the gains compound, and the forwarders who build the layers and new capabilities first will have a clear advantage to set the economics going forward.
This article was sponsored by Zauber.
Want to hear more? Zauber founder Erik Muttersbach joined Charlotte Goldstone on The Loadstar Podcast to discuss where agentic AI really stands in forwarding today, why adoption matters as much as the technology, and how to separate genuine capability from the hype. Watch the episode here.

Quantinuum says a new error-correction result on its Helios quantum computer gives it greater confidence in a 2029 target for Apollo, its planned fault-tolerant system. The company reported 99.9995% logical memory fidelity , equivalent to roughly five failures per million cycles.
“This derisks the industry,” Quantinuum CEO Rajeeb Hazra told The Wall Street Journal . “We now know the recipe for both creating good physical qubits and error-correcting them in a scalable way using the least number of physical qubits to create a logical qubit.”
Logical Error Rate scaling with color code distance. The green line indicates Quantinuum Helios’ projected logical error rate. The pink line indicates a superconducting architecture’s projected logical error rate. (Quantinuum)
In its color-code experiments, Quantinuum reported an average twelvefold reduction in logical memory errors as code distance increased. Higher code distances allow stronger error protection by using more physical qubits. Extrapolating from those results, the company estimates that its approach could support 100 logical qubits using approximately 30,000 physical qubits, compared with roughly 900,000 for the superconducting color-code implementation it analyzed.
“The paper demonstrates real, serious performance gains from quantum error correction—a logical qubit nearly 100x better than its component physical qubits,” said Robin Blume-Kohout, co-director of Sandia National Laboratories’ Quantum Performance Lab, in Quantinuum’s announcement. Blume-Kohout was not involved in Quantinuum’s study.
In his interview with the Journal , Hazra cited chemistry research as an example of how improved error correction could support commercial applications. The Quantinuum CEO said that the current level of fidelity could support algorithms for making predictions about simple molecules, with the potential for more complex algorithms as accuracy improves.
“We are focused on commercialization, and all the use cases we see have different requirements for fault tolerance,” he said. “That’s why it is so fundamentally important versus just a scientific pursuit.”
Quantinuum’s Roadmap as of 2026.
The technical roadmap also carries financial importance. Quantinuum raised nearly $1.7 billion in its June initial public offering , but reported a $65.4 million loss on $8 million in revenue in its most recent quarter.
Before Apollo, Quantinuum plans to introduce Sol , 2D-grid-based quantum computer. Lessons from Helios are intended to guide its development.
Hazra told the Journal that combining accurate physical qubits with scalable error correction gives Quantinuum greater confidence in its schedule.
“That is what underpins our roadmap confidence of getting to full fault tolerance by 2029,” he said.
Read Quantinuum’s in-depth blog post for more details.
